signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: A post-void residual bladder scan measures the urine left after voiding, quantifying incomplete emptying.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: A patient with storage LUTS and no red flags has failed conservative measures. Which drug class is appropriate?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: Storage symptoms / overactive bladder are treated with an antimuscarinic or mirabegron.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Which systemic condition should be considered when LUTS includes marked polyuria with thirst and weight loss?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: Marked polyuria with thirst and weight loss suggests diabetes mellitus (or diabetes insipidus) rather than a primary bladder cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Before checking a PSA in a man with LUTS, what should be done?
options: Counsel the patient about the implications of the result
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: PSA testing requires counselling about its limitations and implications; recent infection, DRE or ejaculation can also raise it.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Which two bedside assessments are mandatory in the initial evaluation of LUTS?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: A DRE (prostate) and urinalysis (infection, blood, glucose) are mandatory first-line assessments.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A 75-year-old man cannot pass urine for 8 hours and has severe suprapubic pain with a palpable, tender bladder. What is the immediate management?
options: Urethral catheterisation and record the residual volume
Oral alpha-blocker and review in a week
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Acute retention is relieved by immediate catheterisation, recording the drained residual volume, before investigating the cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A man in acute urinary retention also reports numbness around the perineum, weakness in both legs and new faecal incontinence. What is the priority after catheterisation?
options: Urgent MRI to exclude cauda equina
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg weakness and faecal incontinence indicates cauda equina — an emergency needing urgent MRI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: After catheterising a man with high-pressure chronic-on-acute retention (creatinine raised, bilateral hydronephrosis), what must be monitored?
options: Urine output and U&E for post-obstructive diuresis
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Decompressing high-pressure retention can cause a post-obstructive diuresis — monitor urine output and U&E and replace fluids.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Which medication class most commonly precipitates acute urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Anticholinergic drugs (along with opioids and decongestants) commonly precipitate acute retention.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A man in acute retention is draining heavily blood-stained urine with clots via the catheter, which then blocks. What is the appropriate catheter?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Clot retention requires a 3-way catheter with irrigation to clear clots and keep the catheter patent.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Why should a PSA test be avoided during an episode of acute urinary retention?
options: Retention and catheterisation falsely raise the PSA
PSA is only useful in women
PSA cannot be measured with a catheter
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Acute retention, catheterisation, UTI and DRE all raise PSA, so the test should be deferred.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: What single feature best distinguishes acute from chronic urinary retention?
options: Chronic retention is always smaller volume
Acute retention never needs a catheter
Acute retention is painful; chronic is painless
Acute retention causes no bladder distension
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Acute retention is painful; chronic retention is painless and typically high-volume.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A 70-year-old man in acute retention is found to have a hard, irregular prostate on DRE. What does this suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: A hard, nodular prostate suggests prostate cancer (a smooth enlarged prostate suggests BPH); investigate with PSA/MRI/biopsy once settled.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Following catheterisation for BPH-related acute retention, which medication is started to improve the chance of a successful trial without catheter?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: An alpha-blocker started before a trial without catheter improves the likelihood of successful voiding.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: What volume of urine is typically drained on catheterisation in acute retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Typically 500–1000 mL is drained, and relief of the pain confirms the diagnosis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Besides prostatic causes, which common precipitant should be actively sought and treated in acute retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Constipation is a common, reversible precipitant of acute retention and should be treated.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A woman develops acute urinary retention 12 hours after a normal vaginal delivery. What is the most likely explanation?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Post-partum retention is a recognised transient cause; catheterise and it usually resolves.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A 78-year-old man is found to have a hugely distended but painless bladder, dribbling incontinence and a creatinine of 320 with bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound. What is the diagnosis?
options: Low-pressure chronic retention with normal kidneys
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A painless distended bladder with hydronephrosis and renal impairment is high-pressure chronic retention — the dangerous form.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: After catheterising a patient with high-pressure chronic retention, 4 litres drain and urine output remains very high. What must be done?
options: Monitor U&E and urine output and replace fluids (post-obstructive diuresis)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A post-obstructive diuresis can lose litres — monitor U&E and output and replace fluids to prevent hypovolaemia.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Which feature distinguishes chronic from acute urinary retention?
options: Chronic retention always has a smaller residual
Chronic retention only occurs in women
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Chronic retention is painless and high-volume; acute retention is painful.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: An adult man reports new bed-wetting at night. Combined with a palpable bladder and a raised creatinine, what does this suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Nocturnal enuresis in an adult with a palpable bladder and renal impairment is a hallmark of high-pressure chronic retention.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A patient has continuous urinary dribbling and a large palpable bladder. How is this best understood?
options: Overflow incontinence due to chronic retention
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Continuous dribbling from a chronically over-distended bladder is overflow incontinence due to retention — drain the bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Which investigation best distinguishes high-pressure from low-pressure chronic retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Renal-tract ultrasound (hydronephrosis) and U&E determine whether the retention is high-pressure and threatening the kidneys.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: What is the most common cause of chronic urinary retention in men?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is the commonest cause of chronic retention in men.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A diabetic patient with a large residual and an atonic bladder on urodynamics has chronic retention. What is the appropriate long-term management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A neurogenic / atonic bladder is best managed with intermittent self-catheterisation to empty the bladder regularly.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Why is a rapid trial without catheter usually inappropriate in high-pressure chronic retention?
options: It commonly recurs and threatens the kidneys, needing definitive management
It is only used in women
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: High-pressure retention typically recurs and endangers renal function, so long-term drainage or definitive surgery is preferred over a quick TWOC.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: What bladder finding is characteristic of chronic retention on examination?
options: A painless, palpable, dull suprapubic mass
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Chronic retention gives a painless, palpable, dull suprapubic bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A man with chronic retention has a hard, irregular prostate on DRE. What must be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A hard, nodular prostate raises concern for prostate cancer — investigate with PSA, MRI and biopsy.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Which complication of chronic obstruction should be actively screened for at diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Longstanding obstruction can cause obstructive uropathy and chronic kidney disease — check renal function and imaging.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A 52-year-old woman leaks small amounts of urine when she coughs, sneezes or exercises, but has no urgency. What type of incontinence is this and what is first-line treatment?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Leakage on effort without urgency is stress incontinence; pelvic-floor muscle training is first-line.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A 60-year-old man has a sudden strong urge to void followed by leakage, with frequency and nocturia. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A sudden urge then leakage with frequency/nocturia is urgency incontinence from an overactive bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A frail man has continuous dribbling of urine and a palpable bladder; the post-void residual is 900 mL. What is the mechanism?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A palpable bladder with a large residual indicates overflow incontinence due to chronic retention — treat the retention.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A woman has constant, uncontrollable urinary leakage that began after a difficult hysterectomy. What is the most likely cause?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Continuous leakage after pelvic surgery suggests a vesicovaginal fistula, requiring investigation and surgical repair.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: An 85-year-old with dementia and poor mobility wets herself because she cannot get to the toilet in time; her urinary tract is otherwise normal. What type of incontinence is this?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Functional incontinence is leakage from an inability to reach the toilet despite a normal urinary tract.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: Which bedside test is most important to exclude overflow before treating incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A post-void residual excludes overflow incontinence from retention, which would change management.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: First-line management of an overactive bladder after conservative measures fail includes which drug class?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Overactive bladder / urgency incontinence is treated with an antimuscarinic or mirabegron after bladder training.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: The mnemonic DIPPERS is used to remember what in the context of incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: DIPPERS lists the reversible/transient causes (Delirium, Infection, atrophic vaginitis, Pharmaceuticals, Psychological, Endocrine, Restricted mobility, Stool impaction).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A woman with both leakage on coughing and episodes of urge-related leakage is diagnosed with which type?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Features of both stress and urgency indicate mixed incontinence.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A patient develops new incontinence with numbness around the perineum and weakness in both legs. What is the priority?
options: Urgent MRI to exclude cauda equina
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: New incontinence with saddle anaesthesia and bilateral leg weakness is cauda equina — an emergency needing urgent MRI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: Which is the recommended surgical option for stress incontinence in a woman who has failed conservative treatment?
options: Artificial urinary sphincter as first choice
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A mid-urethral sling (or colposuspension) is used for stress incontinence after conservative measures fail.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: An older woman presents with new urinary incontinence, dysuria and cloudy urine. What should be done before further incontinence work-up?
options: Treat the urinary tract infection (a reversible cause)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A UTI is a reversible (DIPPERS) cause — treat it before pursuing a full incontinence work-up.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: A ward patient with a urinary catheter suddenly stops draining urine and becomes anuric. What is the first action?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: A blocked catheter is the commonest cause of sudden ward anuria — flush or replace it first.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An oliguric post-operative patient is hypotensive with dry mucous membranes; urine is concentrated with a low sodium. What is the most likely type of AKI?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Hypovolaemia with concentrated, low-sodium urine indicates pre-renal AKI, which should respond to restored perfusion.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An AKI patient has a potassium of 6.9 mmol/L with peaked T waves on ECG. What is the immediate priority?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes needs IV calcium for cardiac protection, then insulin–dextrose and salbutamol to shift potassium.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An oliguric patient has muddy-brown granular casts on urine microscopy and did not respond to a fluid challenge, following a period of hypotension. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Muddy-brown granular casts with no fluid response after ischaemia indicate acute tubular necrosis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An anuric patient is found to have a palpable bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound. What is the management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Post-renal obstruction is reversible — decompress with a catheter (outlet) or nephrostomy (ureteric).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: Which set of criteria indicates the need for urgent dialysis in AKI?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: The AEIOU criteria (refractory acidosis, hyperkalaemia, intoxication, fluid overload, uraemia) indicate urgent dialysis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: A patient develops AKI with a rash, fever and eosinophilia two weeks after starting a new antibiotic. What is the most likely cause?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: A drug-related AKI with rash, fever and eosinophilia is typical of acute interstitial nephritis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: Which combination of drugs is most nephrotoxic and should be stopped in AKI?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: The NSAID + ACE inhibitor (± diuretic) "triple whammy" is a classic nephrotoxic combination to stop in AKI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: A patient with AKI after a prolonged period lying on the floor has a very high creatine kinase and dark urine. What is the mechanism?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: A raised CK with dark (myoglobin) urine after immobility indicates rhabdomyolysis causing AKI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: Which bedside assessment most directly guides fluid management in oliguria?
options: Volume status (BP, JVP, mucous membranes, oedema)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Assessing volume status determines whether the patient is fluid-deplete (pre-renal, give fluids) or overloaded (restrict / consider dialysis).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An oliguric patient has blood and protein on dipstick with red-cell casts and hypertension. What category of AKI is this?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Blood, protein and red-cell casts with hypertension indicate an intrinsic (glomerular) cause — investigate for glomerulonephritis/vasculitis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: After confirming pre-renal AKI, besides giving fluids, what is an essential step?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Stopping nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, etc.) is essential alongside restoring perfusion in pre-renal AKI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: A 19-year-old presents with polyuria, marked thirst, weight loss and a capillary glucose of 28 mmol/L with ketones. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and hyperglycaemia with ketones in a young person is DKA (type 1 diabetes).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: What is the most appropriate first investigation in a patient with polyuria and polydipsia?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Blood glucose is checked first because diabetes mellitus is the commonest cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: A patient on long-term lithium has polyuria with dilute urine that does not concentrate after desmopressin. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI — the kidney does not respond to ADH, so urine fails to concentrate even after desmopressin.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: During a water deprivation test, a patient fails to concentrate their urine but then concentrates it well after desmopressin. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Concentrating only after desmopressin indicates cranial DI (ADH deficiency that responds to replacement).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: A patient with polyuria is confused and constipated, with a corrected calcium of 3.2 mmol/L. What is the underlying problem?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Polyuria with confusion and constipation and a high calcium indicates hypercalcaemia ("bones, stones, abdominal groans, psychic moans").

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: A young woman with a psychiatric history drinks large volumes of water and has dilute, high-volume urine; on water deprivation her urine concentrates normally. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Urine that concentrates normally on deprivation in a high water-drinker indicates primary polydipsia.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: A patient develops severe polyuria the day after transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. What is the most likely cause and key risk?
options: Cranial diabetes insipidus with risk of hypernatraemia
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Pituitary surgery can cause cranial DI; uncorrected water loss risks hypernatraemia, so sodium and fluid balance are monitored.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: Which treatment is used for cranial diabetes insipidus?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Cranial DI is treated with desmopressin (synthetic ADH).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: Which finding on urinalysis suggests an osmotic diuresis is the cause of polyuria?
options: Ketones alone in a well patient
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Glycosuria reflects the glucose driving an osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: What paradoxically reduces urine volume in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
options: A thiazide diuretic (with a low-salt diet)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: A thiazide (with salt restriction) paradoxically reduces polyuria in nephrogenic DI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: An older patient has profound polyuria, a glucose of 45 mmol/L, severe dehydration and no significant ketones. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Very high glucose with profound dehydration and minimal ketones in an older patient is HHS.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.question: Which test best confirms diabetes mellitus as the cause of polyuria?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Polyuria & Po.explanation: Blood glucose / HbA1c confirms diabetes mellitus, the commonest cause of osmotic polyuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: A patient reports frothy urine. Dipstick shows protein +++. What is the most appropriate next step to quantify it?
options: Albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) on an early-morning sample
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Proteinuria is quantified with an ACR (or PCR) on an early-morning urine sample.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: A 5-year-old has periorbital oedema, heavy proteinuria, a low albumin and high cholesterol. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: A child with the nephrotic tetrad most commonly has minimal change disease, usually steroid-responsive.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops sudden flank pain and haematuria with a rising creatinine. What complication should be suspected?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is prothrombotic (antithrombin loss); renal vein thrombosis presents with flank pain, haematuria and worsening renal function.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: An older man has renal failure, anaemia, bone pain and a corrected calcium of 3.0, but the urine dipstick is negative for protein. What must be sent?
options: Serum and urine electrophoresis / free light chains
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Myeloma proteinuria (free light chains) is dipstick-negative — send electrophoresis and serum free light chains.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: Which finding indicates a nephritic rather than a nephrotic picture?
options: Haematuria with red-cell casts, hypertension and AKI
Heavy proteinuria with a low albumin
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: A nephritic picture features haematuria (red-cell casts), hypertension and AKI; nephrotic features heavy protein loss and oedema.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: Which drug class is first-line to reduce proteinuria and slow renal decline?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: ACE inhibitors / ARBs reduce proteinuria and slow progression of renal disease.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: A long-standing diabetic has proteinuria and background retinopathy. What is the most likely renal diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Proteinuria with diabetic retinopathy in a long-standing diabetic indicates diabetic nephropathy.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: A healthy 17-year-old has proteinuria on a daytime sample but none on a first-morning (recumbent) sample. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Proteinuria present when upright but absent when recumbent is benign orthostatic proteinuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: Which complication of nephrotic syndrome results from urinary loss of immunoglobulins?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Loss of immunoglobulins in nephrotic syndrome increases the risk of infection.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: A young woman has proteinuria, a malar rash, arthralgia and low complement. What renal diagnosis is likely?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Proteinuria with a malar rash, arthralgia and low complement suggests lupus nephritis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: In an adult with unexplained nephrotic syndrome, which investigation typically establishes the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: A renal biopsy is usually needed to define the cause of unexplained nephrotic syndrome in adults.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.question: Which is the commonest cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria overall in adults?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Frothy Urine.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is the commonest overall (secondary) cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria in adults.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 6-year-old is brought in with puffy eyes that are worst in the morning and mild ankle swelling. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: A child with periorbital oedema worse on waking plus heavy proteinuria is nephrotic syndrome, and in children the commonest cause is minimal change disease (usually steroid-responsive).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 40-year-old has a unilateral red swollen eyelid, pain on eye movement, proptosis and a fever. Which is the priority investigation?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: Unilateral painful proptotic swelling with fever is orbital cellulitis — sight-threatening. Urgent CT orbits with IV antibiotics and ophthalmology/ENT input is required.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 55-year-old presents with facial and neck swelling, dilated veins over the chest wall, and breathlessness that worsens when bending forward. What is the most likely underlying cause?
options: Superior vena cava obstruction from malignancy
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: Facial/neck swelling with distended chest-wall veins and positional breathlessness is SVC obstruction, most often caused by a mediastinal malignancy such as lung cancer.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 30-year-old develops swelling of the lips and eyelids with an urticarial rash and wheeze minutes after eating peanuts. What is the immediate treatment?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: This is anaphylaxis. The first-line treatment is IM adrenaline, followed by antihistamine, steroid and ABC support.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 62-year-old on ramipril presents with recurrent episodes of lip and periorbital swelling without any itch or urticaria. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue ramipril and add an antihistamine
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: Angioedema without urticaria in a patient on an ACE inhibitor is bradykinin-mediated ACEi angioedema. It responds poorly to adrenaline/antihistamines; the key step is to stop the ACE inhibitor.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 50-year-old has non-pitting periorbital puffiness, cold intolerance, weight gain and a heart rate of 52. What single test is most useful?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: Non-pitting periorbital puffiness with cold intolerance, weight gain and bradycardia suggests hypothyroidism (myxoedema); thyroid function tests confirm it.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 68-year-old man has bilateral periorbital and ankle oedema, a raised JVP and orthopnoea. Which mechanism best explains his oedema?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: A raised JVP with orthopnoea points to congestive cardiac failure and fluid overload, rather than a renal, hepatic or allergic cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 45-year-old presents with bilateral painless periorbital oedema. Dipstick shows no protein and no blood; serum albumin is low; he has ascites, jaundice and spider naevi. What is the mechanism?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: Low albumin without proteinuria, alongside ascites, jaundice and spider naevi, indicates chronic liver disease causing hypoalbuminaemia and reduced oncotic pressure.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 35-year-old woman notices frothy urine and puffy eyes each morning. Blood tests show albumin 22 g/L and cholesterol is markedly raised. What is the best next investigation to quantify the problem?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: The picture is nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia). Quantify the proteinuria with an ACR or protein:creatinine ratio.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: Which combination of features most reliably points AWAY from a renal cause and towards a cardiac cause of periorbital oedema?
options: Raised JVP with orthopnoea and ankle oedema
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: A raised JVP with orthopnoea and dependent ankle oedema indicates fluid overload from cardiac failure. Frothy urine/proteinuria points to the kidney and non-pitting puffiness to the thyroid.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: A 25-year-old develops an itchy, scaly, red left upper eyelid two days after starting a new eye cream. There are no systemic features and the urine is clear. What is the most likely cause?
options: Allergic contact dermatitis of the eyelid
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: A localised, itchy, unilateral eyelid reaction after a new topical product, with no systemic upset, is allergic contact dermatitis rather than a fluid or infective cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.question: An adult is confirmed to have nephrotic syndrome with no obvious secondary cause. Which investigation is usually needed to guide treatment?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Periorbital O.explanation: In adults with unexplained nephrotic syndrome a renal biopsy is usually required to determine the histological type (e.g. membranous, FSGS) and guide immunosuppression; children are often treated empirically for minimal change disease first.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A 16-year-old has sudden severe left scrotal pain. The testis is high-riding and lies transversely, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: This is testicular torsion. It is a clinical diagnosis and requires scrotal exploration within 6 hours to save the testis — do not delay for imaging.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A 24-year-old notices a painless, firm lump within the right testis that does not transilluminate. What is the most important investigation?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: A solid intratesticular lump is testicular cancer until proven otherwise. Urgent scrotal ultrasound plus tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH) is required.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A 40-year-old has a painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates brightly, and the testis cannot be felt separately from it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: A fluctuant, brightly transilluminating swelling that surrounds the testis (so it cannot be palpated separately) is a hydrocele.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A 30-year-old presents with a new right-sided 'bag of worms' varicocele that does not decompress when he lies down. What should you do next?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: A new, right-sided, or non-decompressing varicocele may be caused by a renal mass obstructing venous drainage. Image the kidneys to exclude renal cell carcinoma.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A 55-year-old has a scrotal swelling you cannot get above, with a cough impulse and audible bowel sounds. It is soft and reducible. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: A swelling you cannot get above, with a cough impulse and bowel sounds, extending from the groin, is an inguinoscrotal hernia. Reducibility indicates it is not (yet) strangulated.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A 22-year-old has a tender, swollen epididymis, fever and urethral discharge; pain is relieved by elevating the testis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: Gradual onset with a tender epididymis, fever, discharge and relief on elevation suggests epididymo-orchitis (often STI-related in young men). If any doubt remains, torsion must still be excluded by exploration.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: Which single examination finding most reliably separates an epididymal cyst from a hydrocele?
options: Whether it is separate from the testis
Whether there is a cough impulse
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: Both transilluminate. The distinguishing feature is location: an epididymal cyst is separate from (above and behind) the testis, whereas a hydrocele surrounds it.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A 60-year-old has an irreducible, tender inguinoscrotal swelling with vomiting and abdominal distension. What does this indicate?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: Irreducibility, tenderness and features of bowel obstruction indicate a strangulated hernia — a surgical emergency.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: Why is a firm or irregular testis important even when there is an associated hydrocele?
options: A reactive hydrocele can conceal an underlying testicular tumour
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: A secondary (reactive) hydrocele can form around a testicular tumour or infection. A firm or irregular testis must be imaged with ultrasound.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: In which of the following scrotal presentations is ultrasound the WRONG first move?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis needing immediate exploration; waiting for an ultrasound risks losing the testis. Ultrasound is appropriate for the other presentations.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: A boy presents with a small tender lump at the upper pole of the testis and a bluish discolouration through the skin ('blue-dot sign'), with the rest of the testis non-tender. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Testicular torsion of the whole testis
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: A localised tender upper-pole nodule with a blue-dot sign suggests torsion of a testicular appendage — a milder mimic of torsion, though whole-testis torsion must still be excluded if there is doubt.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.question: Which tumour markers are most useful when investigating a suspected testicular tumour?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Scrotal Swell.explanation: AFP, β-hCG and LDH are the key markers for testicular germ-cell tumours, aiding diagnosis, staging and monitoring.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 15-year-old wakes with sudden severe left scrotal pain and vomiting. The left testis is high and lies horizontally, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the correct management?
options: Trial of antibiotics and reassess in 24 hours
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: This is textbook testicular torsion. It is a clinical diagnosis requiring exploration within ~6 hours; imaging should not delay surgery.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 26-year-old has 3 days of gradually worsening right scrotal pain with fever, dysuria and urethral discharge. Pain eases when the testis is lifted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: Gradual onset with fever, dysuria, discharge and relief on elevation (Prehn positive) indicates epididymo-orchitis, likely STI-related at this age.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has severe scrotal and perineal pain out of proportion to findings, with skin crepitus, a dusky patch and a lactate of 4. What is the diagnosis and priority?
options: Fournier's gangrene; resuscitation and emergency debridement
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: Pain out of proportion with crepitus, dusky skin and sepsis in a diabetic is Fournier's gangrene — a necrotising infection needing resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent surgical debridement.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 17-year-old has acute scrotal pain. The testis lies normally and is non-tender except for a small tender bluish nodule at its upper pole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: A localised upper-pole tender nodule with a blue-dot sign and an otherwise non-tender testis suggests torsion of a testicular appendage, though torsion must still be excluded if there is any doubt.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 30-year-old presents with a tense, exquisitely tender scrotum after a sports injury; the testicular contour is not palpable. What is the best next investigation?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: After trauma with a tense tender scrotum and lost contour, scrotal ultrasound is used to assess for testicular rupture/haematocele; significant injury requires surgical exploration.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 40-year-old has severe colicky pain radiating from the left loin to the groin and scrotum. The testis is normal on examination and urine shows microscopic haematuria. What is the most likely cause?
options: Referred ureteric colic from a stone
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: Colicky loin-to-groin pain with a normal testis and haematuria is referred ureteric colic; a CT KUB confirms the stone.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: Which feature should most strongly push you towards scrotal exploration rather than conservative management?
options: Sudden onset with an absent cremasteric reflex
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: Sudden onset with an absent cremasteric reflex strongly suggests torsion and mandates exploration. Fever, dysuria, discharge and relief on elevation favour epididymo-orchitis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 6-year-old boy has scrotal pain, colicky abdominal pain and a palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and legs. What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: Palpable purpura with abdominal and scrotal pain in a child suggests Henoch-Schönlein purpura; torsion still needs excluding if scrotal signs dominate.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: At scrotal exploration a torted testis is found to be viable after detorsion. What should be done regarding the other testis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: The predisposing bell-clapper anatomy is usually bilateral, so the contralateral testis is fixed (orchidopexy) to prevent future torsion.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: Which statement about Prehn's sign is correct?
options: A positive sign reliably excludes torsion
It is only useful in children
It replaces the need for the cremasteric reflex
It is unreliable and must not override a torsion story
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: Prehn's sign (relief on elevation in epididymo-orchitis) is unreliable; a convincing torsion history warrants exploration regardless.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: A 22-year-old presents with acute pain over a testis in which he had previously noticed a painless hard lump. Ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass with haemorrhage. What is the underlying diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: Acute pain over a pre-existing solid intratesticular lump suggests a testicular tumour that has bled or infarcted; tumour markers and urgent urology referral are required.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.question: An elderly man has an irreducible, tender inguinoscrotal swelling that you cannot get above, with vomiting and abdominal distension. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Scrotal.explanation: An irreducible tender swelling you cannot get above, with obstruction, is a strangulated hernia — a surgical emergency.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A 45-year-old with hypertension has bilateral, knobbly, ballotable flank masses and a family history of kidney disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: Bilateral knobbly ballotable kidneys with hypertension and a positive family history are characteristic of autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A 63-year-old man has a hard, irregular, unilateral ballotable kidney, weight loss and visible haematuria. What is the priority investigation?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: A unilateral hard irregular kidney with haematuria is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise; contrast-enhanced CT is used to characterise and stage the mass.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A 55-year-old has a tender, smooth, enlarged kidney with fever, rigors and a lactate of 4 mmol/L. Imaging shows an obstructing stone with a dilated system. What is the immediate priority?
options: Urgent decompression (nephrostomy or stent) with resuscitation
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: This is pyonephrosis — an infected obstructed kidney. It is a urological emergency requiring resuscitation and urgent decompression alongside antibiotics.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A 3-year-old is found to have a painless, smooth abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Repeated palpation to define its edges
Urgent referral to paediatric oncology, avoiding repeated palpation
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: A painless flank mass in a child suggests Wilms' tumour; it should be referred urgently and palpated as little as possible.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: Which examination feature best distinguishes an enlarged kidney from an enlarged spleen?
options: You can get above a kidney and it is ballotable
The kidney is dull to percussion
The kidney has a palpable notch
The kidney does not move with respiration
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: You can get above a kidney and it is ballotable and resonant (overlying bowel); a spleen has a notch, is dull, is not ballotable, and you cannot get above it.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A 70-year-old man has bilateral smooth enlarged kidneys, a palpable bladder and a poor urinary stream. What is the mechanism?
options: Bilateral hydronephrosis from bladder outflow obstruction
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: Bilateral hydronephrosis with a palpable bladder and poor stream indicates bladder outflow obstruction (e.g. prostatic), causing back-pressure on both kidneys.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A patient has a smooth, non-tender mass in the right iliac fossa with an overlying scar. What is it most likely to be?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: A smooth non-tender iliac-fossa mass with an overlying scar is a transplanted kidney, which is placed extraperitoneally in the pelvis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: Which of the following is a recognised paraneoplastic feature of renal cell carcinoma?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma can cause polycythaemia (via erythropoietin), as well as hypercalcaemia, pyrexia and hypertension.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: What is the most appropriate first-line imaging for an enlarged, ballotable kidney of uncertain cause?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: Renal ultrasound is first line: it readily distinguishes cysts, hydronephrosis and solid masses, guiding further imaging such as CT.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A patient with ADPKD should be considered for screening of which associated abnormality, particularly with a relevant family history?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: ADPKD is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms; screening is considered where there is a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: A single palpable kidney is found in a patient whose other kidney is congenitally absent. What is the most likely explanation for the enlargement?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: A solitary functioning kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy and may become palpable without any pathology.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.question: Which combination most strongly indicates that an obstructed kidney needs emergency decompression rather than elective treatment?
options: Enlargement plus fever, rigors and sepsis
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Enlarged / Ba.explanation: Fever, rigors and sepsis with an obstructed kidney indicate pyonephrosis, which mandates emergency decompression alongside antibiotics and resuscitation.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A 68-year-old man has a hard, irregular, craggy prostate with loss of the median sulcus. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and review in a year
Refer on a suspected-cancer pathway for PSA, MRI and biopsy
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: A hard, irregular prostate with a lost median sulcus is prostate cancer until proven otherwise and warrants urgent referral for PSA, multiparametric MRI and biopsy.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A 55-year-old man has fever, rigors, perineal pain and an exquisitely tender, boggy prostate. What should you avoid during the examination?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: This is acute bacterial prostatitis. Vigorous prostatic massage can provoke bacteraemia and should be avoided; treat with urine culture and antibiotics.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A 70-year-old man has a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, rubbery prostate with the median sulcus preserved, and obstructive urinary symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: A smooth, symmetrical, rubbery prostate with a retained median sulcus and obstructive LUTS is typical of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: When is the best time to take a PSA sample in relation to a DRE?
options: Before the DRE (or not immediately after)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: A DRE can transiently raise PSA, so it is best taken before (or not immediately after) examination, and deferred during active infection.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A man with known prostatitis remains febrile with swinging temperatures despite 5 days of appropriate antibiotics, and the prostate feels fluctuant. What is the likely complication?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: Persisting swinging fever with a fluctuant prostate despite antibiotics suggests a prostatic abscess, which requires imaging and drainage.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A 72-year-old man has an enlarged prostate, a palpable non-tender bladder, poor stream and a post-void residual of 700 mL, with a rising creatinine. What does this indicate?
options: Chronic urinary retention with obstructive uropathy
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: A large painless residual with renal impairment indicates chronic urinary retention causing obstructive uropathy; the obstruction must be relieved to protect the kidneys.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: Which single DRE feature most strongly favours malignancy over benign enlargement?
options: A hard, irregular surface with loss of the median sulcus
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: A hard, irregular surface with loss of the median sulcus favours cancer; symmetrical rubbery enlargement with a retained sulcus favours BPH.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A 66-year-old man has a hard prostate, PSA of 85 ng/mL and new thoracic back pain. What is the most appropriate investigation for the back pain?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: A hard prostate with a very high PSA and new bone pain suggests skeletal metastases; a bone scan (with ALP) assesses for metastatic disease.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: Which is the most appropriate first-line medical treatment to relieve moderate obstructive LUTS from BPH quickly?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: An alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin) relaxes prostatic smooth muscle and relieves symptoms quickly; a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor works over months and is added for larger glands.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A 40-year-old man has months of pelvic and perineal pain. The prostate feels near-normal and repeated urine cultures are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: Persistent pelvic/perineal pain without infection or a clearly abnormal gland is chronic pelvic pain syndrome (chronic prostatitis/CPPS).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: Why is prostate size on DRE a poor determinant of treatment in BPH?
options: Because DRE cannot assess the prostate
Because symptom severity correlates poorly with gland size
Because only urologists can examine it
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: Symptom severity correlates poorly with prostate size, so management is guided by symptoms, flow and residual volume rather than the size felt on DRE.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.question: A man presents with a painful, palpable, tender suprapubic mass and inability to pass urine, with an enlarged prostate on DRE. What is the immediate management?
options: Oral alpha-blocker and review in clinic
Urethral (or suprapubic) catheterisation to relieve acute retention
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pros.explanation: This is acute urinary retention; immediate catheterisation relieves the obstruction and pain, after which the underlying prostatic cause is managed.
